lead: Colorado homes deal with hail, frozen pipes and fast spring runoff. DryFlare helps owners on the Front Range and in the mountains dry out after water gets in.
risk: hail-damaged roofs, frozen pipes and flash floods
why: The Front Range is one of the most hail-prone areas in the country. Denver, Aurora and Colorado Springs see damaging hail most summers. Cracked shingles or skylights often leak days later. Afternoon storms can also turn dry creeks into torrents. The September 2013 floods hit Boulder, Lyons and Estes Park hard.

Winter adds frozen pipes, most often when it drops from the 50s to below zero in a day. Basements are common along the Front Range, so a burst pipe or a failed sump pump often means a finished basement full of water. Mountain homes and rentals sit empty for weeks, so a small leak can run for days. Wyoming and Utah share many of these risks.
image_alt: Frozen water spilling from a building drain pipe
image_caption: Sudden cold snaps on the Front Range split pipes in walls and basements.
problems: Denver metro, Colorado Springs, Fort Collins
tips: Shut off outside spigots and remove hoses before the first hard freeze.
Put water sensors and an auto shut-off valve in rental and vacation homes.
Have the roof checked after any hail storm.
Test your sump pump and add a battery backup if the basement is finished.
insurance: Many Colorado policies use a percentage deductible for wind and hail. A roof claim may cost you more than a pipe burst.

faq.q: Is a frozen pipe burst covered in Colorado?
faq.a: Usually, if it was sudden and the home was kept heated. Policies may deny freeze claims if the house was left unheated or vacant for a long time. Keep heat on and shut off water before long trips.

licensing: Colorado has no statewide general contractor license. Cities and counties such as Denver license builders. Plumbers and electricians hold state licenses.
